paragraphs.heading: A chart of the stars
paragraphs.text: A Hertzsprung–Russell diagram, or H–R diagram, is a scatter plot that sets each star's luminosity or absolute magnitude against its spectral class or effective temperature. Ejnar Hertzsprung created it in 1911, and Henry Norris Russell, working on his own, did so in 1913. It was a major step toward understanding how stars evolve.

paragraphs.heading: Reading the layout
paragraphs.text: Every version shares the same basic layout. More luminous stars sit toward the top, and hotter stars sit toward the left. The original put spectral type along the horizontal axis and absolute visual magnitude up the vertical one. Spectral type is not a number, but the order of the types follows surface temperature steadily.

paragraphs.heading: Several versions
paragraphs.text: Observers often use a color–magnitude diagram, which swaps spectral type for a color index such as B-V. For a star cluster, whose members all lie at about the same distance, the vertical axis can simply be how bright the stars appear, because one constant, the distance modulus, separates apparent from absolute magnitude for every member. Theorists instead plot effective temperature against luminosity, almost always on log-log scales, and their models of stellar structure produce plots that match observations. Converting between the two forms is hard: it needs a color–temperature relation, a bolometric correction, the distance, and corrections for interstellar reddening and extinction.

paragraphs.heading: The main sequence
paragraphs.text: Most stars fall along a band called the main sequence. Low-mass stars sit at its cooler, dimmer end, and more massive stars at its hotter, brighter end. While stars are on this line, they are fusing hydrogen in their cores.

paragraphs.heading: Giants and the gap
paragraphs.text: Higher up than the main sequence sits a prominent group of cool stars that are larger and more luminous: the red giants. They include stars fusing hydrogen around an inert helium core, stars fusing helium in their cores, and stars burning both hydrogen and helium in shells that surround a core that is largely inert. Between the red giants and the main sequence lies the Hertzsprung gap, home to subgiants, between spectral types A5 and G0.

paragraphs.heading: How the idea grew
paragraphs.text: In the nineteenth century, Harvard College Observatory classified tens of thousands of stars from photographed spectra, leading to the Henry Draper Catalogue. Antonia Maury also sorted stars by the width of their spectral lines, and Hertzsprung took narrow lines as a sign of greater luminosity. In 1910 Hans Oswald Rosenberg plotted stars of the Pleiades by apparent magnitude against the strength of lines that track temperature. Since those stars share one distance, his chart was in effect luminosity against temperature, and such diagrams are still used for clusters today.
